baselineSnapshot.label: History
baselineSnapshot.title: A history that others kept writing
baselineSnapshot.description: Six historians carry a chronology from the ancient world into the early Middle Ages.

nodes.name: Julius Africanus
nodes.detail: Africanus brought biblical and other chronologies into a universal history. His work survives in fragments; Eusebius names him among the earlier Christian chronographers he consulted.

nodes.name: Eusebius
nodes.detail: Eusebius draws on Africanus and other predecessors, arranging the histories of different peoples into a comparative chronology. This is a documented use of sources, not a teacher-student relationship.

nodes.name: Jerome
nodes.detail: Jerome translates Eusebius into Latin, adds material on Roman history and continues the account to 378. His preface explains his dual role as translator and author.

nodes.name: Prosper of Aquitaine
nodes.detail: Prosper abridges and continues the Eusebius-Jerome chronicle. Successive versions carry the account into his own century; the fullest reaches 455.

nodes.name: Victor of Tunnuna
nodes.detail: Victor continues Prosper's chronicle from 444 to 566/567, with particular attention to church politics. The overlapping years reflect the versions used by the continuators.

nodes.name: John of Biclar
nodes.detail: John begins where Victor ends and carries the narrative to 590. His own preface names Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper and Victor as the predecessors whose chronological sequence he is continuing.

baselineSnapshot.label: Languages & texts
baselineSnapshot.title: The English Bible, generation by generation
baselineSnapshot.description: A Greek edition becomes an English translation, then a succession of revisions.

nodes.name: Desiderius Erasmus
nodes.detail: Erasmus publishes a printed Greek New Testament with a Latin translation. Tyndale later consults its revised editions of 1519 and 1522.

nodes.name: William Tyndale
nodes.detail: Tyndale uses Erasmus's Greek text in producing his English New Testament. His later revisions and Old Testament work feed into subsequent English Bibles.

nodes.name: John Rogers
nodes.detail: Published under the name Thomas Matthew, this Bible combines Tyndale's work with Coverdale's. It brings together material from more than one translator, rather than simply reprinting Tyndale.

nodes.name: Miles Coverdale
nodes.detail: Coverdale revises Matthew's Bible for the Great Bible. The new edition becomes the basis for another official revision under Matthew Parker.

nodes.name: Matthew Parker & team
nodes.detail: Parker oversees a revision of the Great Bible. The Bishops' Bible later serves as the prescribed base text for the King James translators.

nodes.name: King James translators
nodes.detail: The translators use the Bishops' Bible as their base, consulting Tyndale, Matthew, Coverdale, the Great Bible and Geneva. This milestone brings several earlier streams together.

nodes.name: Revision committees
nodes.detail: The Revised Version's preface explicitly describes its New Testament as a revision of the 1611 translation. Its Old Testament follows in 1885.

baselineSnapshot.label: Archaeology & places
baselineSnapshot.title: Jericho: an interpretation tested and retested
baselineSnapshot.description: Excavation, disagreement and new measurements reshape the dating of one city's destruction.

nodes.name: Sellin & Watzinger
nodes.detail: Ernst Sellin and Carl Watzinger undertake an early major excavation at Tell es-Sultan. Later teams return to the same site with new methods and questions.
nodes.sourceLabel: UCL: history of excavation at Jericho

nodes.name: John Garstang
nodes.detail: Garstang returns to Jericho and interprets the destruction of City IV in relation to Joshua, proposing a date around 1400 BCE. This is his interpretation of the evidence.

nodes.name: Kathleen Kenyon
nodes.detail: Kenyon re-excavates the site and places the destruction of the fortified Bronze Age city earlier, around the end of the Middle Bronze Age. Her conclusions challenge Garstang's identification.

nodes.name: Bryant G. Wood
nodes.detail: Wood re-examines the published evidence and argues for a later destruction date around 1400 BCE, challenging Kenyon's chronology. His proposal becomes the subject of a published exchange.

nodes.name: Piotr Bienkowski
nodes.detail: Bienkowski directly disputes Wood's reassessment and defends a Middle Bronze Age destruction. The disagreement concerns the interpretation and dating of archaeological material.

nodes.name: Bryant G. Wood
nodes.detail: Wood answers Bienkowski's objections in the same journal issue. These are two opposing readings of the evidence, not successive stages of consensus.

nodes.name: Bruins & van der Plicht
nodes.detail: High-precision radiocarbon measurements of cereals and charcoal add an independent test of the destruction chronology. This is new evidence on the same question, rather than a personal reply to Wood.

baselineSnapshot.label: Reference works
baselineSnapshot.title: A Hebrew lexicon, rebuilt across two centuries
baselineSnapshot.description: Follow a reference work through new languages, expanded editions and a new way to look up words.

nodes.name: Wilhelm Gesenius
nodes.detail: Gesenius publishes his Hebrew-German lexicon. His continuing lexicographical work produces revised manuals and a larger thesaurus, rather than a single unchanging dictionary.

nodes.name: Wilhelm Gesenius
nodes.detail: The Latin manual carries Gesenius's lexicographical work to an international readership. This is the edition Robinson subsequently translates into English.

nodes.name: Edward Robinson
nodes.detail: Robinson publishes an English translation of the 1833 Latin manual. BDB's preface identifies this translation as an earlier foundation for English-language Hebrew study.

nodes.name: Edward Robinson
nodes.detail: Robinson revises his English Gesenius. The later BDB editors identify 1854 as the last revision, explaining why a new lexicon had become necessary.

nodes.name: Brown, Driver & Briggs
nodes.detail: The three editors build a new lexicon on Gesenius as translated by Robinson, also consulting the larger thesaurus and later scholarship. Their names belong together at this collaborative milestone.

nodes.name: Hendrickson edition
nodes.detail: A later edition codes BDB to the numbering system of Strong's concordance. It links two reference tools; it does not mean Strong authored or revised the original BDB.

baselineSnapshot.label: Theology & philosophy
baselineSnapshot.title: Can an idea establish that God exists?
baselineSnapshot.description: An argument is challenged, answered and reformulated across nine centuries.

nodes.name: Anselm of Canterbury
nodes.detail: Anselm reasons from the idea of a being than which none greater can be conceived. His argument prompts an objection from another monk, Gaunilo.

nodes.name: Gaunilo
nodes.detail: Gaunilo challenges the inference from a conceived object to its existence, using the example of an excellent island. His reply directly addresses Anselm's argument.

nodes.name: Anselm of Canterbury
nodes.detail: Anselm answers Gaunilo and defends the distinctive reasoning of the Proslogion. The reply is preserved alongside the original argument and objection; the exact dates of this exchange are approximate.

nodes.name: René Descartes
nodes.detail: Centuries later, Descartes presents a different ontological argument based on perfection and necessary existence. This is a later formulation of the question, not a claim that he derived it from Anselm's reply.

nodes.name: Immanuel Kant
nodes.detail: Kant attacks ontological proofs, including the Cartesian approach, arguing that existence is not a real predicate that adds a property to a thing's concept.

nodes.name: Norman Malcolm
nodes.detail: Malcolm accepts the force of the existence-as-perfection objection but distinguishes another argument in Anselm involving necessary existence. He reopens the discussion in modal terms.
nodes.sourceLabel: Stanford: modal versions of the argument

nodes.name: Alvin Plantinga
nodes.detail: Plantinga examines modern modal arguments and develops a version using possible worlds and maximal greatness. The crucial possibility premise remains part of the philosophical debate.
